extracted.intended_audience: employers, workplace safety and health professionals, compliance officers, and state OSHA program staff in the United States
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of U.S. federal and state regulatory requirements, recommended standards, and interpretive guidance governing occupational heat exposure, employer duties, PPE, recordkeeping, and training. Intended to inform compliance, planning, and prevention of heat-related illness in workplaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer responsibilities — General Duty Clause (Section 5(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the General Duty Clause, Section 5(a)(1) of the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970, employers are required to provide their employees with a place of employment that 'is free from recognized hazards that are causing or likely to cause death or serious harm to employees.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have interpreted this to mean employers have a legal obligation to provide a workplace free of conditions or activities that either the employer or industry recognizes as hazardous and that cause, or are likely to cause, death or serious physical harm to employees when there is a feasible method to abate the hazard. This explicitly includes heat-related hazards that are likely to cause death or serious bodily harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow NIOSH recommended standard for occupational heat stress
rubrics_metrics.description: NIOSH has published 'Criteria for a Recommended Standard – Occupational Exposure to Heat and Hot Environments' (DHHS/NIOSH Publication No. 2016-106) with recommendations for employers about how to prevent heat-related illnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA points employers to the NIOSH document as a source of criteria and recommendations for preventing heat-related illness; employers should consult and consider implementing NIOSH recommendations as part of their heat-prevention programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: California Heat Illness Prevention Standard (state-specific requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: California's Heat Illness Prevention Standard requires employers to provide training, water, shade, and planning. A temperature of 80°F triggers the requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers operating in California must comply with Cal/OSHA's specific requirements (training, access to potable water, shaded rest areas, and heat illness prevention planning) once ambient temperature meets the trigger; see CalOSHA and full text of the California heat standard for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-specific heat exposure standards (CO, MN, OR, WA, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several states have their own heat exposure standards or rules (examples listed: Colorado Agricultural Labor Conditions Rules for heat; Minnesota standard applying to indoor places of employment; Oregon Heat Illness Prevention materials and General Occupational Safety and Health regulations; Washington Outdoor Heat Exposure Rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State Plans may adopt standards covering hazards not addressed by federal OSHA; employers should consult the full text of each state's regulations and guidance for sector- and jurisdiction-specific requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: State Plans must be at least as effective as federal OSHA
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA-approved State Plans operate workplace safety and health programs for their states/territories and are required to have standards and enforcement programs that are at least as effective as OSHA's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State Plans may have different or more stringent requirements than federal OSHA; employers in State Plan states must follow the applicable state standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: PPE hazard assessment and PPE selection/communication (29 CFR 1910.132(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: 29 CFR 1910.132(d) requires every employer in general industry to conduct a hazard assessment to determine the appropriate PPE to be used to protect workers from the hazards identified in the assessment. (Also referenced: sector analogues 29 CFR 1915.152, 1917.95, 1926.28 and 1926.95.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation mandates that the employer perform a hazard assessment; select and mandate worker use of necessary PPE; communicate selection decisions to workers; and select PPE that properly fits the employees. See sector-specific PPE provisions for shipyard, maritime, and construction applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping requirements for heat-related injuries and illnesses (29 CFR 1904)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Recordkeeping regulation (29 CFR 1904) requires employers to record certain work-related injuries and illnesses when cases involve days away from work, restricted work activity/job transfer, or medical treatment beyond first aid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA clarifies the difference between first aid and medical treatment per 29 CFR 1904.7(b)(5) (example: IV fluids meet the general recording criteria; being instructed to drink fluids does not). Under 29 CFR 1904.39, employers must report to OSHA all work-related fatalities within eight hours and all work-related inpatient hospitalizations within twenty-four hours; this includes occupational heat-related events such as heat illness, heat stroke, kidney injury, and rhabdomyolysis that result in death or inpatient hospitalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitation standards require potable water (sector citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various sanitation standards require employers to provide potable water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited sanitation regulations include 29 CFR 1910.141 (general industry), 29 CFR 1915.88 (shipyard), 29 CFR 1917.127 (maritime), 29 CFR 1918.95, 29 CFR 1926.51 (construction), and 29 CFR 1928.110 (agriculture). Employers should ensure access to potable water consistent with these standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical services and first aid training/availability (sector citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical Services and First Aid standards require that persons on-site be adequately trained to render first aid in the absence of medical facilities within close proximity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited provisions include 29 CFR 1910.151 (general industry), 29 CFR 1915.87 (shipyard), 29 CFR 1917.26 (maritime), 29 CFR 1918.97, and 29 CFR 1926.50 (construction). Employers should ensure appropriate first-aid training and access where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety training and education requirements for construction (29 CFR 1926.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Safety Training and Education standard for construction (29 CFR 1926.21) sets requirements for training construction employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers in construction must provide safety and health training appropriate to hazards (including heat hazards) per 1926.21; consult the standard for training scope and content expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of Interpretation and enforcement guidance on heat-related topics
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA letters of interpretation and guidance documents address specific heat-related questions (examples listed on the page include: use of hard hats while working on roofs in hot weather; whether PPE is mandatory under heat stress conditions; clarification of preexisting injury/illness and recordkeeping; wearing short-sleeved shirts during thermal spray operations with hexavalent chromium exposure; requirements for 'nature breaks' and weather-related 'comfort breaks'; acceptable methods to reduce heat stress hazards; fire retardant PPE requirements and PPE hazard assessment; PPE requirements during marine oil spill response; landscaping employees working in extreme temperatures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These letters provide case-specific clarifications and identify feasible and acceptable methods to reduce heat stress. Employers should consult the cited letters for topic-specific interpretations and precedent that inform compliance and enforcement expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable methods to reduce heat stress hazards (identified in guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA has identified feasible and acceptable methods that can be used to reduce heat stress in workplaces (referenced letter dated October 17, 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers should consider the methods identified in OSHA's guidance (engineering controls, administrative controls, PPE selection, work/rest cycles, hydration, shade, training, etc., as applicable) and implement feasible measures to abate heat hazards under the General Duty Clause or applicable standards.
